replies.body: A custom story's 'Ways to play it' could bet against the story right above it. Live, the lithium story said Albemarle gains (a rival of Lithium Americas, whose costs jumped) while the play under it bet Albemarle falls: two separate AI reads. Now the idea engine is told the story's own read and never bets a name the other way, so the brain's graded call agrees with the card too. Plays saved earlier today are checked when shown (the lithium one now shows LAC and LIT, not ALB). 'Big move' plays are left alone. No research, gates or grading changed.

replies.re: Custom stories should find where the change goes and how to play it (live chat)
replies.body: Done, all three. 1) 'Who it moves' now looks past the searched company: 3-5 names including at least one indirect play (a supplier, rival, customer or theme ETF), tagged 'indirect'. 2) The story's last card and its card on the News page show 'Ways to play it': the idea engine's top 3 picks (buy the shares, or an options version), practice money only. 3) Each new custom story's idea is saved as one of the brain's own calls and graded against the S&P 500 at 7, 30 and 90 days, so the brain learns whether ideas from searches pay off. Extra cost is about a tenth of a cent per story.

replies.re: Custom AI story from search (via chair)
replies.body: Search can now make a brand-new story. Type anything on the News page ("uranium", "Costco earnings", a ticker) and tap "Make a story about this". The app pulls that subject's real headlines from the past 14 days, the AI writes a story in the same Story-mode cards (hook, what happened, why it matters, the twist, who it moves, believe or doubt), and it opens right away. A new last card, "Where this comes from", lists the real headlines it was built from, and numbers on the cards must be written in those headlines. If there's no real news on it, it says so and writes nothing. Cost stays small: each subject is written once a day and shared with everyone, 5 new stories per person a day, 150 for the whole app. Live test result follows below once the deploy is up. Tested on the live site on a phone-size screen: 'Costco earnings' made a story from 2 real headlines (Mizuho raising its target to $1,150 from $1,100 on stockpiling sales); 'lithium' made one from 5 real headlines about Lithium Americas' Thacker Pass cost estimate rising to $3.83 billion from $2.93 billion, with LAC and ALB; 'uranium' honestly said there's nothing recent (our news source's newest uranium-company headline is 18 days old). Good queries for the promo: lithium or Costco. Two Story-mode fixes from the test: when the text is long, the number charts get their own card so nothing runs off a phone screen, and the % badges on them are no longer green or red, since a cost going up 31% isn't good news.

The first big numbers on the Brain page were the flattering ones. The scorecard said 53% of our #1 picks beat the S&P 500 and the #1 led our other ideas by +1.2 pts (in green), and then the paragraph under it said to read that as too generous, because those practice calls scored each stock with results that came later. A finance professor would stop at the headline. The tiles now show the version we stand behind, our #1 rebuilt without that peek: 52% beat the S&P (+1.5 pts average) and +0.5 pts over our other ideas, on 2,703 test calls, the same version the luck check judges just below. A small line under them still gives the stored numbers with the peek. The +0.5 is no longer green, since it isn't clear of luck yet. No research, gates or grading changed.

The Brain page's luck check was seven dense paragraphs, a wall on a phone. It now opens with 'At a glance': one line per check with a tick, a cross or a '~', all about the same honest version of our #1 (rebuilt without the look-ahead peek), and a one-line verdict. Today it reads: ahead of our other ideas by +0.5 pts on 2,703 test calls, but not clear of luck (t 1.7, and 1.0 counting overlapping calls, against a bar of 3.3); partly carried by a few huge calls; ahead in 3 of 4 stretches but behind in the latest; the 7-day real-time results are too early. The full paragraphs are one tap away under 'How each check works'. One thing the paragraphs hid: 'the lead is broad, not a few lucky calls' was true of the stored #1 (its 10 best calls are 27% of its lead), but without the peek its 10 best calls are 73% of a smaller lead. The page now says both. No numbers, gates or grading changed.

Agent HQ is easier to use from your phone. There's a 'Write to the team' button at the top that jumps to the message box (it was below 12 to-do items, 9 agent cards and the whole thread). 'Needs you' shows the newest 4 with 'Show all'. Replies no longer say 're #(no new messages)': a routine report says 'update', and an answer to one of your messages quotes the start of what you wrote. I also fixed the thread dropping an agent's newest replies once it had more than 10. Nothing you've sent through HQ has arrived yet (the table is empty); sending works when I test it, so a short hello there will reach everyone.

Research now tries 'many weak signals, one vote'. Several of our ways to pick the #1 each carry a little real information, but we only ever judged them one at a time, and the leader keeps changing. Now, for each test period, the research takes the ways that had a clear lead (t 2 or more) on calls made at least 90 days earlier, up to 8, drops near-copies, and gives each one an equal vote with no fitted weights. It's scored on the same test calls as everything else and counts as one more try for the luck bar. The Brain page says how it compares with the typical and the best single way, and which ways it kept most often. If it beats them all, that's evidence the brain should combine ways rather than pick one. Reporting only: today's #1, the gates and grading are unchanged. Numbers appear after the next research run. First live run (20:36 UTC, 2,703 test calls): the average beats our other ideas by +0.6 pts (t 1.0 counting overlap honestly), ahead in 3 of 4 stretches, better than 21 of 34 single ways but well short of the best (negative coskewness, t 3.1). It mostly kept momentum-style ways, so for now combining doesn't add an edge of its own.

Search is on the News page. Type a company ("nvidia"), a ticker (NVDA or $nvda) or a topic ("oil", "chips"). A company shows its price and today's move, its latest headlines, and buttons for Close Call and making a call on it; below that, every story we picked in the past 7 days that moves it or mentions it. A topic shows the matching stories. Nothing found says so and offers to ask about it in chat. The app starts keeping a week of stories from this deploy, so for the first few days search covers fewer stories. No AI cost per search.

Close Call fix: 'Will NVDA close above $125 on Dec 4?' read 46% with NVDA at $129.17, $4 above the line, and the nearby lines jumped around (56% at $124, 42% at $126). The weekend option quotes were set while NVDA traded near $125.80, so measured against $129.17 every put looked expensive and every call cheap, and the safety check that should have caught that measured its allowance with the puts' inflated volatility, so it let the quotes through. Now the app reads the volatility at the price the quotes were set at (where calls and puts agree, about 103% instead of the feed's 122%), uses it for the odds at today's price, and says the quotes were set as if NVDA were near $125.78. On this weekend's quotes: $124 55%, $125 54%, $126 52%, $128 49%, $130 45%. SPY, whose quotes fit its price, is unchanged. Practice money only; grading unchanged.

Price Check and Close Call overstated option volatility whenever the market was closed. This weekend SPY's options for Nov 27 read '42% yearly volatility, expensive, 2.45x realized'. Those prices are Friday's closing quotes, which still cover the risk from Friday's close to the expiration, but the data feed divided them by the 5 days left from Sunday. Measured from Friday's close, the same prices are about 36%. The app now works the volatility out from each option's own bid and ask, timed from when the quotes were set (now while the market is open, otherwise the last close, with holidays and early closes counted), and Price Check says when it's showing closing quotes. Close Call's 'how far it could move' range is unchanged, because that comes from the prices; only the yearly-volatility label beside it changes. Odds, trades and grading are unchanged.
